code.title: Immutable strings: every change makes a new object
code.python:
import time

s = "hello"
t = s.upper()                      # a new object; s is untouched
print(s, t, s is t)

parts = [str(i) for i in range(20000)]

start = time.perf_counter()
out = ""
for p in parts:
    out += p                       # may copy the growing string each time
slow = time.perf_counter() - start

start = time.perf_counter()
joined = "".join(parts)            # one pass, O(n) total
fast = time.perf_counter() - start

print("same result:", out == joined, "length:", len(joined))
print("join is not slower:", fast <= slow * 5)

followUps:
Collect the small pieces in a list and call "".join(parts) once at the end. That takes one pass over the data, so it is O(n) time, and the list plus the final string are the only memory.

For example, 100,000 pieces of 10 bytes make 1 MB: append each piece to a list (100,000 cheap appends), then one join allocates 1 MB and copies each piece once. Using s += piece in a loop can copy the growing string every time, which is O(n²) in the worst case.

io.StringIO is an in-memory text file: you can write() to it and later read everything with getvalue(). It is useful when code expects a file object, for example csv.writer, print(..., file=buf) or a test that needs fake input.

It is also an alternative to list plus join for building big strings: buf.write(piece) repeatedly, then buf.getvalue(). Writes are amortised O(1), so the total is O(n). io.BytesIO is the bytes version.

code.title: Slicing with negative values and clamping
code.python:
s = "abcdef"
print("s          :", s)
print("s[1:4]     :", s[1:4])        # start included, stop excluded
print("s[-3:]     :", s[-3:])        # last three characters
print("s[::2]     :", s[::2])        # every second character
print("s[::-1]    :", s[::-1])       # reversed
print("s[-2:-5:-1]:", s[-2:-5:-1])  # walk backwards from index -2
print("s[2:1000]  :", s[2:1000])    # out of range is clamped
print("s[10:]     :", repr(s[10:])) # empty string, no error

try:
    print(s[1000])                  # indexing is strict
except IndexError as e:
    print("IndexError:", e)

try:
    print(s[::0])                   # step 0 makes no sense
except ValueError as e:
    print("ValueError:", e)

print(slice(1, 5, 2).indices(len(s)))

followUps:
It is "edc". Start -2 means index 4 ('e'), the step -1 walks left, and stop -5 means index 1, which is excluded. So we collect indexes 4, 3, 2: 'e', 'd', 'c'.

The rule: with a negative step, the slice runs from start leftwards until it reaches stop without including it. If start were to the left of stop with a negative step, the result would be empty.

slice(1, 5, 2).indices(n) turns the slice into three concrete non-negative numbers (start, stop, step) for a sequence of length n, after applying defaults, negative indexes and clamping.

Example: slice(-3, None, None).indices(6) returns (3, 6, 1), and slice(2, 1000).indices(6) returns (2, 6, 1). It helps when you write your own __getitem__ for a custom sequence: use range(*key.indices(len(self))) to get the exact indexes to visit.

code.title: str versus bytes and the Unicode sandwich
code.python:
text = "caf\u00e9 \U0001F600"
data = text.encode("utf-8")        # str -> bytes (exit of the sandwich)
print("text :", text, "len", len(text))
print("bytes:", data, "len", len(data))

back = data.decode("utf-8")        # bytes -> str (entry of the sandwich)
print("round trip ok:", back == text)

try:
    text + data                    # mixing the two is an error
except TypeError as e:
    print("TypeError:", e)

bad = b"caf\xe9"                   # latin-1 bytes are not valid UTF-8
try:
    bad.decode("utf-8")
except UnicodeDecodeError as e:
    print("UnicodeDecodeError:", e.reason)
print("replace:", bad.decode("utf-8", errors="replace"))
print("latin-1:", bad.decode("latin-1"))

followUps:
Python counts code points, JavaScript counts UTF-16 code units. The emoji U+1F600 is one code point, so Python says 1. It lies outside the 16-bit range, so UTF-16 stores it as a surrogate pair (two units), and JavaScript's length says 2.

In JavaScript, [..."😀"].length gives 1 because the iterator walks code points. Neither counts what a user sees as one character (grapheme), e.g. a flag or an emoji with skin tone is several code points.

Mojibake is garbled text such as cafÃ© instead of café. It happens when bytes were encoded with one codec but decoded with another, typically UTF-8 bytes read as Latin-1 or cp1252.

To repair, reverse the mistake: bad.encode("latin-1").decode("utf-8") turns cafÃ© back into café. The real fix is to decode with the right codec at input; the library ftfy can guess repairs for existing damaged data.

code.title: UTF-8 byte lengths and safe truncation

followUps:
Encode to bytes, cut at 255, then move the cut left while the byte at the cut position is a continuation byte (it starts with bits 10). Then decode the prefix.

b = s.encode("utf-8")
cut = 255
while cut > 0 and (b[cut] & 0xC0) == 0x80:
    cut -= 1
result = b[:cut].decode("utf-8")

At most 3 steps back are needed, since a character has at most 4 bytes. Cost is O(n) for the encode and O(1) for the search.

utf-8-sig reads and writes UTF-8 with a byte order mark (BOM), the three bytes EF BB BF at the start of a file. Windows tools such as Notepad and Excel often add it to mark the file as UTF-8.

Decoding with plain utf-8 leaves an invisible \ufeff at the start of the first string, which breaks things like the first CSV column name. Decoding with utf-8-sig strips it. Encoding with it adds the BOM, which helps Excel open the file correctly.

code.title: Four ways to format a string
code.python:
from string import Template

name, score = "Asha", 91.456

print(f"f-string : {name} scored {score:.1f}")
print(f"debug    : {score=}")
print("format   : {} scored {:.1f}".format(name, score))
print("percent  : %s scored %.1f" % (name, score))
print(Template("template : $who scored $pts").substitute(who=name, pts=score))

class Money:
    def __init__(self, cents):
        self.cents = cents
    def __format__(self, spec):    # f"{obj:spec}" lands here
        if spec == "usd":
            return "$%d.%02d" % divmod(self.cents, 100)
        return str(self.cents)

print(f"custom   : {Money(1999):usd} or {Money(1999)}")

# format() with user text can reach attributes; Template cannot
print("unsafe   :", "{0.__class__.__name__}".format(name))

followUps:
With logging.info(f"user {u}") the string is built every time, even when INFO is disabled. With logging.info("user %s", u) the logger only formats the message if the record is actually emitted.

If a debug call sits in a hot loop of 1,000,000 iterations and debug logging is off, the f-string version still pays 1,000,000 formatting costs; the lazy version pays almost nothing. Linters flag it (rule G004) for that reason, and because structured logging backends can group messages by the unformatted template.

It defines the method __format__(self, spec). The text after the colon is passed to it as a string, and it returns the final text.

class Temp:
    def __init__(self, c): self.c = c
    def __format__(self, spec):
        return f"{self.c * 9/5 + 32:.1f}F" if spec == "f" else str(self.c)

Then f"{Temp(100):f}" gives "212.0F". If you do not define it, object.__format__ accepts only an empty spec and raises TypeError otherwise. Built-ins like datetime define their own specs.

code.title: What with does: __enter__ and __exit__

followUps:
When the process dies without running Python code: os._exit(), a hard kill (SIGKILL), a power cut or a crash of the interpreter. Also if __enter__ itself raises, because the block was never entered, so __exit__ is not called.

Ordinary exceptions, return, break and sys.exit() (which raises SystemExit) all do run __exit__. Example: if the process is killed after writing 10 KB, the unflushed buffer is lost, so critical data needs flush plus fsync.

Use contextlib.ExitStack. It collects context managers at run time and closes all of them, in reverse order, even if one fails.

with ExitStack() as stack:
    files = [stack.enter_context(open(p)) for p in paths]
    # use files; all are closed on exit

If opening the 3rd of 5 files fails, the first two are still closed. A plain list of open() calls without it would leak those handles.

code.title: Stream a big file: constant memory
code.python:
import io
from collections import deque, Counter

# stand-in for a huge log file; real code would use open("big.log")
log = io.StringIO("".join("10.0.0.%d GET /p%d\n" % (i % 4, i) for i in range(1, 11)))

tail = deque(maxlen=3)             # keeps only the last 3 lines
ips = Counter()
count = 0
for line in log:                   # one line at a time, O(longest line) memory
    count += 1
    tail.append(line.rstrip())
    ips[line.split()[0]] += 1

print("lines:", count)
print("last 3:", list(tail))
print("hits per ip:", dict(ips))

# binary files: fixed-size chunks with the walrus operator
data = io.BytesIO(b"x" * 2500)
total = 0
while chunk := data.read(1000):
    total += len(chunk)
print("bytes read in chunks:", total)

followUps:
Open it in binary mode, seek to the end, and read backwards in blocks until you have seen 10 newlines. This touches only the last few KB, so it is O(size of the tail) rather than O(100 GB).

f.seek(0, 2); pos = f.tell(); data = b""
while pos > 0 and data.count(b"\n") <= 10:
    step = min(4096, pos); pos -= step
    f.seek(pos); data = f.read(step) + data

Then split on newlines and take the last 10. The simple alternative, deque(f, maxlen=10), is also constant memory but must read all 100 GB.

Use a fixed-size summary or split the work. An exact set of 1 billion IPv4 addresses is too big (several GB), but IPv4 fits a bitmap: 2^32 bits is 512 MB, one bit per possible address.

If even that is too much, hash each IP into 16 partition files, then count unique values per partition one at a time (each fits in RAM) and add the counts. For an approximate answer, HyperLogLog counts billions of distinct items with about 12 KB and roughly 1 percent error.

code.title: Open modes and an atomic rewrite
code.python:
import os, tempfile

with tempfile.TemporaryDirectory() as d:
    path = os.path.join(d, "f.txt")

    with open(path, "w", encoding="utf-8") as f:
        f.write("one\n")
    with open(path, "a", encoding="utf-8") as f:       # append keeps old data
        f.write("two\n")
    print("after a:", open(path, encoding="utf-8").read().split())

    try:
        open(path, "x")                                # exclusive create
    except FileExistsError:
        print("x refused: file exists")

    with open(path, "w", encoding="utf-8"):            # w truncates on open
        pass
    print("after w:", os.path.getsize(path), "bytes")

    # safe rewrite: temp file in the same folder, then atomic replace
    tmp = path + ".tmp"
    with open(tmp, "w", encoding="utf-8") as f:
        f.write("new content\n")
        f.flush()
        os.fsync(f.fileno())                           # force it to disk
    os.replace(tmp, path)
    print("after replace:", open(path, encoding="utf-8").read().strip())

followUps:
The csv module handles line endings itself, including newlines inside quoted fields. If the file is opened without newline="", Python's own newline translation also acts, so on Windows \r\n can become \r\r\n (blank rows) and an embedded newline in a quoted cell can be altered on reading.

With newline="", Python passes the text through untouched and csv sees the exact bytes. The csv docs say to always open csv files this way.

flush() moves Python's buffered data to the operating system, which is enough for another program to read it. os.fsync(fd) asks the OS to push its own cache to the physical disk, which is what survives a power failure.

Example: after f.write("x"), the byte may sit in Python's buffer; after flush() it is in the OS cache; only after os.fsync(f.fileno()) is it safely on disk. Fsync is slow (milliseconds), so use it only for data you cannot lose.

code.title: What import does: sys.modules, finders, loaders

followUps:
Because it lets a module that is only half run still be found by others. If A imports B and B imports A, the second request finds A already in sys.modules and receives the partial module instead of starting an endless loop of imports.

So import A inside B works (you get the module object, filled in later), while from A import X fails if X is defined after A's import of B. If execution fails, Python removes the entry again so the next import retries.

Because sys.path[0] is the script's folder and is searched before the standard library. A file named random.py or json.py next to your script wins, so import random loads your file instead.

Typical symptoms: AttributeError: partially initialized module 'random' has no attribute 'randint'. Fix by renaming your file and deleting its __pycache__. python -c "import random; print(random.__file__)" shows which file was loaded.

code.title: Circular import failure and the fix

followUps:
Run an import-graph tool in CI and fail the build when it finds a cycle. Tools such as import-linter, pydeps or pylint (rule R0401, cyclic-import) read the imports and report loops.

You can also build it yourself: parse each file with ast, collect module-level imports as edges, and run a depth-first search for a cycle. For a project with 500 modules and 3,000 edges that takes well under a second. Add a test that imports every module in a fresh interpreter, which exposes most load-time cycles.

import A only needs the module object, which already exists in sys.modules (partly filled). The name A.X is looked up later, when the code runs and A has finished loading.

from A import X must fetch the attribute X right now, while A is still at its import line. If X is defined below that line, it does not exist yet and you get "cannot import name X from partially initialized module". Example: A line 1 imports B, X defined on line 2; B does from A import X and fails, but import A then A.X inside a function works.

code.title: __name__ guard and running a file as a module
code.python:
import types

SOURCE = """
def main():
    print("  main() running")
print("  module body, __name__ =", __name__)
if __name__ == "__main__":
    main()
"""

print("run as a script (__name__ == '__main__'):")
exec(SOURCE, {"__name__": "__main__"})

print("imported as a library (__name__ == 'mylib'):")
mod = types.ModuleType("mylib")
exec(SOURCE, mod.__dict__)         # body runs, main() does not
print("calling it explicitly:")
mod.main()

print("this file's own __name__:", __name__)
print("this file's __package__ :", repr(__package__))

followUps:
It is when a file ends up imported twice under two names: once as __main__ (because you ran it) and again by its real name when another module imports it. You then get two separate copies of its classes and globals, so isinstance checks fail and module state is duplicated.

Example: you run python pkg/app.py, and pkg/util.py does import pkg.app. The file runs twice, once as __main__, once as pkg.app. Avoid it by running python -m pkg.app and keeping entry points thin.

A console_scripts entry point in pyproject.toml, such as mytool = "pkg.cli:main", makes the installer create an executable called mytool. That small launcher imports pkg.cli by name (like -m) and calls main().

So the code runs as an imported module, with proper package context and relative imports, and __name__ is pkg.cli, not __main__. The if __name__ == "__main__" block is not used on that path, so keep logic in main().

code.title: Packages, __init__ and __all__
code.python:
import sys, types

# build a tiny package in memory: pkg, with submodule pkg.tools
pkg = types.ModuleType("pkg")
pkg.__path__ = []                         # marks it as a package
sys.modules["pkg"] = pkg

exec("""
print("  pkg/__init__ runs once")
__all__ = ["public"]
def public(): return "public API"
def helper(): return "internal"
""", pkg.__dict__)

tools = types.ModuleType("pkg.tools")
tools.__package__ = "pkg"
sys.modules["pkg.tools"] = tools
pkg.tools = tools
exec("def double(x): return x * 2", tools.__dict__)

ns = {}
exec("from pkg import *", ns)             # __all__ limits what star exports
print("star import gives:", sorted(k for k in ns if not k.startswith("__")))
print("pkg.helper() still reachable:", pkg.helper())
print("submodule call:", sys.modules["pkg.tools"].double(21))
print("is a package:", hasattr(pkg, "__path__"), "| tools is:", hasattr(tools, "__path__"))

followUps:
__all__ is a list of names that from package import * exports. Without it, star-import takes every public name (no leading underscore) in the module namespace.

Example: a module defines public and helper with __all__ = ["public"]; from m import * gives only public. It does not make names private, since m.helper still works. It also documents the intended public API for tools and readers.

To make import bigpkg fast. If __init__.py imported every heavy submodule (numpy-backed code, for example), every user would pay that cost, even when they use one function.

Module-level __getattr__ (PEP 562) loads a submodule only when first accessed:

def __getattr__(name):
    if name == "plot":
        import importlib
        return importlib.import_module(".plot", __name__)
    raise AttributeError(name)

If importing takes 800 ms eagerly, lazy loading can cut start-up to a few ms.

code.title: Peek inside a virtual environment
code.python:
import venv, os, sys, tempfile

print("outside a venv:", sys.prefix == sys.base_prefix)

with tempfile.TemporaryDirectory() as d:
    env = os.path.join(d, ".venv")
    venv.create(env, with_pip=False)          # no network needed
    print("top level:", sorted(os.listdir(env)))
    with open(os.path.join(env, "pyvenv.cfg")) as f:
        for line in f:
            key = line.split("=")[0].strip()
            if key in ("include-system-site-packages", "version"):
                print("pyvenv.cfg:", line.strip())
    bindir = "Scripts" if os.name == "nt" else "bin"
    print(bindir + "/ has python:", any(n.startswith("python") for n in os.listdir(os.path.join(env, bindir))))
    # a venv is just a folder, so deleting it removes the whole environment
print("deleted with the temp folder")

followUps:
Because it is large, machine-specific and fully rebuildable. It holds absolute paths and links to the Python on your machine, so it does not work on another computer or OS.

A typical environment is 50 to 500 MB of third-party files, which bloats the repository forever once committed. Commit instead pyproject.toml and a lock file (uv.lock, requirements with pinned versions), add .venv/ to .gitignore, and recreate it with one command.

uv is written in Rust, resolves dependencies in parallel, and reuses a global cache of downloaded wheels. It also installs files by hard-linking or copying them from that cache rather than unpacking and compiling again, and it does not start Python or pip to create the venv.

So a cached install of 50 packages can take well under a second, compared with many seconds for pip. Creating an empty venv takes milliseconds because it only writes pyvenv.cfg and a launcher.

code.title: Verifying artifacts with pinned hashes

followUps:
~= is the compatible release operator: ~=2.31 means >=2.31, ==2.*, and ~=2.31.1 means >=2.31.1, ==2.31.*. It allows newer fixes but not the next major (or minor) version.

Use it when a project follows semantic versioning and you want bug fixes automatically but fear breaking changes. Example: ~=1.4.2 accepts 1.4.9 but not 1.5.0. Note ~=2 is invalid; it needs at least two parts.

Because a library is installed together with other libraries in someone else's environment. If your library requires requests==2.31.0 exactly and another one needs 2.32.0, the resolver cannot satisfy both and installation fails.

Libraries should declare wide ranges such as requests>=2.31,<3, the lowest version you test plus a cap at the next major. Applications own the final environment, so they pin exact versions in a lock file for reproducible deployments.
